newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syria's Assad holds little hope for peace process.
newsitem.headline: Syria's Assad holds little hope for peace process.

text.p: Syrian President Hafez al-Assad voiced pessimism over prospects of Middle East peace after talks in Damascus on Tuesday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
"It is difficult for me to say there is hope in light of the current situation," Assad told a joint news conference with Mubarak at the end of a previously unannounced meeting in Damascus.
"I don't think there is anyone who knows what is happening and could say there is hope...Every day we get a new proof that there is no hope," Assad said.
But the Syrian president said Damascus was still committed to the peace process and wanted to make peace with Israel.
"In light of what we see and hear the best we expect is the continuation of the stalemate until there are new prospects," he said.
Assad said that he discussed with Mubarak the stalled Arab-Israeli peace talks and other regional and bilateral matters and that view points were identical on all issues discussed.
Mubarak said that the alternative for peace would be "dangerous" not only for all the countries who are taking part in the peace process.
No talks have been held between Syria and Israel since Benjamin Netanyahu became prime minister in June last year.
Syria wants Israel to accept full withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967, before resuming peace talks.
The Egyptiun leader said he discussed with Assad the idea of a common Arab market which he said would benefit all Arab states.
"We cannot live in a world of cartels and blocks while we work individually. At the end all of us would be harmed if we do not have a common Arab market," Mubarak said.
Foreign ministers of Syria, Egypt and the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council states approved the idea of setting up a common market among themselves that would be a nucleus for a common Arab market.
The ministers of the so-called Damascus Declaration states, concluding talks in Syria last month, assigned a special committee to discuss the issue.
